newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Jesse Jackson in Brazil to promote Afro ties.
newsitem.headline: Jesse Jackson in Brazil to promote Afro ties.

text.p: U.S. black leader Jesse Jackson urged Brazilians on Tuesday to end racial discrimination and build a "canal" between African Americans and Afro-Brazilians.

In Brasilia at the start of "Black Conciousness Week," Jackson said if Latin America's largest nation broke down racial walls it could shine not just with "Peles" on the soccer field but also in science, the arts and commerce.
"This Afro-Brazilian solidarity tour is designed to connect African Americans and African Brazilians in the diaspora," he told a news conference.

"The Afro-American family has been separated for too long from the Afro-Brazilian family. Now we must ... build a canal between these families. Just as the Panama Canal connects two oceans for trade, we must build a cultural canal."

Jackson arrived in Brasilia on Monday night, held talks with Brazil's Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia and was due to address the Senate on Tuesday. On Wednesday, he was scheduled to meet President Fernando Henrique Cardoso before flying to Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Salvador, the heartland of the Afro-Brazilian revival.

During Brazil's 1964-85 military dictatorship, the existence of racism was denied. But since the establishment of democracy there has been a revival of black consciousness, especially in the northeast. Studies show that blacks, who make up at least 44 percent of the population, suffer poorer living conditions than whites.

The organisers of Jackson's week-long tour, the government-run Palmares Cultural Foundation, said the aim was to stimulate more exchanges between U.S. and Brazilian blacks. They said it was also intended as a recognition of efforts by Cardoso to stamp out discrimination, efforts that Jackson praised lavishly.

The start of his tour was overshadowed by allegations the U.S. consulate in Rio de Janeiro had denied a visa to a 6-year-old mulatto boy because of his skin colour. But Jackson said he had been reassured the incident had nothing to do with racism and had been resolved.
